messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
I slow a half-step so Bram's shield ends up a little ahead of me, and I keep my hands where the man in the apron can see them — thumbs hooked in my belt, nowhere near the sword.

Low, out of the side of my mouth, to Bram and Sefa: "Quarry's gone quiet in the middle of a working day and nobody's run for the road. Tools dropped, not packed. Either everyone got paid off and walked, or something happened and he's standing in the one door with a chimney going." A beat. "Let him talk first. I want to see if he says the word 'case' before we do."

While we cross the yard I'm not looking at him — I'm looking at everything else: the sheds, whether any door hangs open, the lifting frame, the spoil heaps for anyone lying down behind them, boot-prints in the chalk dust and which way they go, and whether there's a cart or a mule track leading out that isn't ours. Also his belt — keys, yes, but is he wearing a blade, and are his knuckles marked.

When we're a comfortable twenty feet off I stop and let Bram do the greeting, but I nod to the man, easy: "Morning, warden. Thorn's shop in Beregost sent us. Quiet day."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Quiet for a working quarry,” I murmur to Pell and Sefa.

I walk toward the house, shield low and sword sheathed, watching the sheds and lower cut as I cross the yard. I stop a few paces from the man, leaving his doorway clear.

“Morning. Bram Halloway. Maela Thorn sent us for a sealed case of dye-salts. Are you the warden?”

I glance toward the abandoned cart. “Work stopped for the day, or is something wrong?”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
"The quiet's wrong," Sefa says quietly to Pell and Bram, her gaze sweeping the yard: the scattered tools, the empty traces. "No one leaves hammers like that unless they left fast, or were taken." She keeps her hands open and away from her dagger, steps forward a few paces toward the house, and raises her voice to the man in the doorway — warm, but watchful.

"Well met. We're sent out from Beregost — Maela Thorn's shop on the Trade Way. She's expecting a sealed case from the warden of Whitestone, and by sunset, if we can manage it. That'd be you?"

Under the friendliness she studies him — the set of his shoulders, his hands, whether he's blocking that doorway like a man at ease or a man standing guard.

scenes.narration:
Pell drops half a step back so that Bram's shield leads, and crosses the yard with his thumbs hooked in his belt. He keeps his eyes off the man in the doorway and on everything else.

There's nothing hidden in the yard. Nobody is lying behind the spoil heaps, and nothing moves on the lifting frame except a loose rope end turning in the breeze. Every shed door is shut but one: a low lean-to at the lip of the lower cut, its plank door standing a hand's width open. The chalk dust has kept a day of footprints. Fifteen or twenty men walked across the yard from the faces and the sheds, all heading the same way, and joined the cart track west toward Beregost. They didn't run. The prints are even and close together, the way men walk in a crowd. A mule's hoofprints go with them. Whatever left here took the road like everyone else, and nothing came back up it except the three of you.

The man in the doorway has no blade. A mason's mallet hangs from a peg inside the doorframe, within easy reach if he wanted it. His knuckles are thick and old-scarred, with white dust worked into the creases, but there are no fresh cuts or swelling. Pell gives him the easy nod from twenty feet out. The man nods back once and says nothing.

Bram stops a few paces short and leaves the doorway clear. The man notices that.

"Osric Hale. Warden." His voice is low and flat, and he doesn't add to it. He looks past Bram at the cart with its empty traces and seems to decide the question deserves an answer. "Stopped yesterday. Noon bell. They walked." A pause. "Three weeks and not a copper from the Gate. I'd have gone with them, if it were mine to walk off."

He tips his chin at the hammers scattered by the lower cut. "Those are the house's tools. They left them where the house can find them. Carter took the mule. He was owed most."

Sefa watches him the whole time he talks. He isn't relaxed, and he isn't afraid either. He stands square in the door like a man who has decided what he's guarding and how far he'll move for it, which isn't far. His eyes are red-rimmed, like someone who sat up late with a lamp and a grievance. Her warmth doesn't soften him. It makes him look at her a moment longer than at the other two, as if he's weighing whether it's real.

"Case is inside," Osric says. "Sealed, the way she wanted it." He doesn't step aside. He rubs a thumb across the dust on his fingers, slowly. "Before it goes anywhere, I want to know something. Your Thorn. Has she paid for it already? And who did she pay?" His jaw works once. "Because it wasn't me. And it wasn't my lads."

Behind him the room is dim. There's a table, a cold mug, a ledger lying open under a stone, and a fire burning low in the grate.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Don’t know,” I say plainly. “She hired us to collect it from you. Ninety gold between us on delivery before sunset. She said nothing about who’d been paid for the salts.”

I settle my shield against my side. “I’ve waited on wages myself. Won’t tell you it’s none of our concern—but I won’t invent an answer to get through your door.”

I nod toward the ledger. “Who owes your lads—the quarry owners, or Thorn? And is there a charge owing on this case, or are you holding it against the missing wages?”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa holds Osric's gaze without flinching, the warmth in her voice settling into something plainer.

"I'll give you a straight answer: I don't know. Thorn hired the three of us yesterday for one thing—to carry that case to her shop by sunset. She pays us only when it's in her hands. She never told me whether the dye-salts were already paid for, or who she'd paid. I won't lie to get through a man's door."

She glances at the empty yard, then back to him.

"But I can offer you the next best thing to coin: a witness at her counter. Walk with us to Beregost and ask her yourself before her buyer's coach leaves, and you'll have all three of us to say we saw you ask. Or if this quarry can't spare you, I'll put your question to her in your name and bring back her answer—plain, whatever it is." A short pause. "If we stand here till sunset, none of us get anything. But before I carry word one, tell me: who should have paid you? The quarry's owner, or some factor in the Gate?"

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
I let the breath out slow. No ambush, just a man who hasn't been paid and is standing on the one thing in this quarry worth anything. I know that man. I've been that man.

"Honest answer, Osric: we don't know. She hired us yesterday evening, told us ninety gold on delivery and not a word about what she paid or to whom. Hirelings don't get shown the ledger." I nod at the open book under the stone behind him. "You've got one, though. If the Gate owes you three weeks, that's the house in Baldur's Gate that owns Whitestone, yes? Not Thorn. She's a shopkeeper buying salts. Chances are her coin went to the house, and the house kept it, same as they kept your lads' wages."

I keep my voice level, not pushing. "So here's how I see it. You can keep the case and the house sends someone less polite than us to fetch it, and you're still not paid. Or the case goes to Beregost today, and you write down what you're owed — your name, the count, the dates — on a sheet from that ledger, and I put it in Thorn's hand myself with the case. She's got a buyer's coach leaving for the Gate tonight. A merchant who wants her salts next month has a reason to lean on the house that a quarryman alone doesn't."

A beat, then plainer: "And I'll be straight — I'm not offering you our ninety. But a man who's kept the fire going and the door shut for a day after everyone walked has done the house's job for it. I'd put that on the sheet too."

While I talk, I'm watching his face — whether the anger's at us or past us, and whether there's something else under it he's not saying. And whether the hand near that mallet peg ever drifts.

Osric hears all three of them out without moving. When Bram says he won't invent an answer, the warden's jaw loosens a little. When Sefa says the same thing in different words, he looks at her again, longer this time. Pell keeps his voice level and watches the man's hands. They stay folded. The right one never goes near the mallet on its peg.

Pell is also watching what's under the anger.

Pell can read the anger, and it goes past them, west toward the road and the Gate beyond it. Whatever else the man is carrying, he keeps it behind his face, and Pell gets no further than the grievance. He gets that much clearly: it's three weeks old and it isn't aimed at the three of them.

"Vandarren," Osric says, answering Bram. "House Vandarren. They own Whitestone on paper. Their factor in the Gate takes the sales, and the wages are supposed to come back down through him." He moves his head slightly toward the ledger. "Four letters I've sent him. Nothing came back. No coin, no reply." He looks at Bram. "Nothing's owing on the case from me. Salt's cut, sealed, ready. The price is the house's business, and I don't see it." A pause. "I'm holding it because it's the only thing at Whitestone anyone wants. That's all."

He turns to Sefa. "Can't walk to Beregost with you. If I leave the gate the house says I abandoned the quarry, and then there's no wages for anybody, ever." He takes that in for a moment, then gives a short nod. "You put the question to her in my name, though. That I'll take."

Pell talks about the shopkeeper and the house, and about someone less polite coming for the case, and Osric's mouth goes tight at the last part. He doesn't argue it. Then Pell mentions the sheet: names, count, dates, put into Thorn's hand with the case. The warden takes his weight off the doorframe for the first time since they came up the track.

"Written down," he says. "Aye. A thing written down goes further than me shouting at a coach." He looks at Pell a moment. "Fifteen men and a carter. Twenty-one days. Plus what I'm owed, if you'll put it on." He doesn't say thank you.

Then he steps out of the door and leaves it open behind him.

He goes in to the table. He lifts the stone off the open ledger, turns to the back, and draws a stub of charcoal from his apron. From the doorway the room is plainer now. There's a cot against the far wall with the blanket still folded square, and a shelf above the grate. On the shelf sits a squat box of dark wood about a foot and a half long, bound at the corners with iron, with three blobs of red wax pressed over the clasp and cord. Osric sits down heavily in front of the ledger. He doesn't write fast. His lips move with the names as he puts them down one under another, the charcoal scratching. Outside, the loose rope end on the lifting frame turns slowly in the wind, and a little chalk dust lifts off the yard and settles again.

messages.text:
Sefa steps just inside the doorway, out of the wind, and watches him work without crowding the table.

"Before you finish that, Osric—tell me the name of the Vandarren factor in the Gate. If Thorn says she's paid him already, I want to know whose name I'm watching her face on." She glances at the iron-bound box on the shelf, then back at the charcoal in his hand. "And when that sheet's done, I'll carry it like it's my own. I'll put it in her hands. Not her errand boy's."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
I let him write. A man putting his own name down for the first time in three weeks doesn't want to be hurried, and I've learned you get a cleaner sheet from someone you don't stand over.

So I don't go to the table. I step inside far enough to be out of his light, nod at the shelf, and ask, "Mind if I look at the case? Not open it — look at it. If I'm carrying it half a day and handing it to a woman who'll check the wax before she checks my face, I want to know what the seals looked like when I took it."

If he grunts assent, I take the box down carefully, keep it where he can see my hands, and turn it in the light from the door: whose seal is on the wax, whether all three impressions match, whether the cord's been cut and re-knotted or the wax sits flat or has been lifted and pressed back. I check the hinges and the iron corners for pry marks, and I heft it — a foot and a half of dye-salt should weigh a certain way, and it should shift like salt, not clink.

While I'm doing that, lightly, so it's conversation and not interrogation: "Your factor in the Gate. He have a name? Thorn's buyer will ask, and so will I if I'm ever stood in his counting-room." A beat. "And Osric — if there's anyone else who knows that case is sitting on your shelf, I'd rather hear it now than on the road."

Then, once I've looked my fill, I set it back exactly where it was and say to Bram and Sefa, "We've got the road to think about. Sun's past the quarter already."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I stay by the doorway while Osric writes, giving Pell room at the table.

“Put the factor’s name on it too, and the dates of those letters. We can promise she hears the claim—not that she pays it.”

I nod toward the box. “Anything we need to know carrying those salts? Keep them dry, away from heat, that sort of thing?”

With Osric’s leave, I check the case’s exterior and wax seals without disturbing them, then judge whether it will ride securely in my pack. “I can carry it. Best we leave you a receipt saying who collected it and that the seals were intact, if they are.”

scenes.narration:
Osric keeps writing while Sefa steps in out of the wind. When she asks for the name, the charcoal stops.

"Pryce. Haddon Pryce." He says it the way a man spits out grit. "Keeps a room off the Wide, over a chandler's. Takes the house's sales, sends the wages down. Supposed to." He writes the name at the top of the sheet in square, careful letters, then looks at her once. "Watch her face, then. I'd like to know what it does."

Bram asks for the dates. Osric grunts and turns pages back through the ledger to find them. Years of tallies go past: blocks cut, carts loaded, men's names with small marks beside them. He finds the place and copies four dates under Pryce's name. There's one for each tenday and the last is three days old. "Hears it," he repeats after Bram, flat. "Aye. That's what I'm buying."

Pell asks about the case and Osric jerks his chin at the shelf. "Look. Keep it where I can see it."

Pell lifts it down slowly and holds it in the light from the door, and Bram leans in beside him. This is Pell's trade, and the box gives him nothing to worry about. The cord goes once around the body and once through the clasp, all one piece, with no cut or re-tied knot. Three seals in red wax sit flat and clean, and the edges have never been lifted. All three carry the same small mark: a mason's square over a W. Pell's eye goes to the ring at Osric's belt, and there among the iron keys hangs a stubby brass seal with the same square cut into its face. The iron corners have rust in their nail-heads and no fresh bright scratches. The hinges have never been pried. The box is heavier than it looks, maybe twenty-five pounds. When Pell tilts it, the weight inside slides a little with a dry, slow hiss like coarse salt in a sack. Nothing clinks.

Bram judges it against his pack. It's too long to go inside. Strapped on top under the flap and lashed at the cord, it will ride well enough, as long as nobody runs.

"Who knows it's here?" Osric repeats Pell's question back to himself. "My lads. The carter. Pryce, he wrote the order. Your Thorn." He thinks about it. "Nobody's come up the track but you three. I'd have seen."

Bram asks how to carry it, and the warden takes a moment over that one.

"Dry. Damp cakes it." The charcoal goes on scratching. "And keep it off a fire."

He doesn't say why. He writes the last line, his own name under the sixteen others, with *twenty-one days* beside it. Then he looks at Bram's offer of a receipt as if it were a strange tool he's deciding whether to trust.

"Receipt." He tears the sheet out along the stitching, carefully, and pushes the ledger an inch across the table toward the door with the back pages open and blank. "Under the names, then. In the house's book. So it's on record who took it."

He lays the torn claim sheet on the table next to where the case sat. He puts the stone on it to keep the draught from lifting it, and rests his flat dusty hand beside it. Pell sets the box back on the shelf exactly where it was. In the grate a log settles and gives off a little smoke, and outside the sun has climbed clear of the eastern lip of the cut.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
I let Bram do the writing — he offered, and a fighter's hand looks more like a man who means it than mine does. When he's done I put my own name under his, plain, no flourish. Pell Dunmore. First time it's gone in anyone's book in six years that wasn't a tally against me.

Then I turn to Osric, because that last bit snagged. "Off a fire — the salts do something? If I'm standing between it and a torch some night I'd like to know whether I'm saving a shopkeeper's profit or my eyebrows."

I nod at the claim sheet under the stone. "Sefa's carrying that. Fold it twice, keep it against your skin, not in the pack — if the pack goes, the sheet shouldn't." To Bram: "Box rides on you, you're the one who won't drop it if we have to move quick. I'll take the rear on the track and keep looking behind us."

To Osric, at the door, as even as I can make it: "You'll hear what her face did. One way or another." Then I'm outside, checking the sun against the western hills, counting hours in my head, and looking down the cart track for anything that wasn't there when we came up it — because the one man in the Gate who knew to send this order is the same man who hasn't sent a copper, and that sits wrong with me.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I take the charcoal and write a plain receipt in the ledger, asking Osric for today’s date: *Collected from Osric Hale for delivery to Maela Thorn of Beregost: one closed wooden case, cord uncut, three Whitestone wax seals intact. Contents not inspected.* I sign it **Bram Halloway**.

Then I lash the case securely atop my pack, using my rope around the box rather than pulling on its sealed cord, and cover it with the flap.

“Your claim goes with us,” I tell Osric, leaving the sheet for Sefa. “Hope the next knock brings your wages.”

Once the others are ready, I head back toward the Beregost track with them, keeping a steady walking pace.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa steps to the edge of the table and reads the claim sheet openly, eyes moving from the sixteen names down to Osric's own, with the four dates under Haddon Pryce. "Seventeen names, twenty-one days. Before I put this in Thorn's hand, give me the number to set beside it. What should those wages have come to—how much a day, in what coin? I'd rather carry a sum she can't shrug off than a list she can call hearsay."

She glances toward the sealed case, then back to Osric, her tone level. "And the salts. 'Keep it off a fire'—is that a carter's rule for any dye, or is there something in that box a flame would settle badly?"

Her hand rests lightly on the edge of the table, not reaching for the sheet yet. "The claim goes into my own hand, and then hers. I won't promise you coin, Osric. I do promise it won't be forgotten in a pocket."

scenes.narration:
Bram takes the charcoal. He writes slowly and doesn't hurry the letters. Osric leans across without being asked and puts the date above the receipt in his own square hand. Then Bram writes underneath: *Collected from Osric Hale for delivery to Maela Thorn of Beregost: one closed wooden case, cord uncut, three Whitestone wax seals intact. Contents not inspected.* He signs it **Bram Halloway**. Pell bends over the book after him and writes *Pell Dunmore* below, plain, with no flourish. Osric reads both lines. He reads the last line twice, then nods once.

He takes Pell's question and Sefa's together, because they're the same question.

"Not a carter's rule." He looks at the box on the shelf rather than at either of them. "Burn a crumb of it and the smoke's sweet. Heavy. Sits in your head like a long day. The low-cut lads used to come up yawning when the lamps hung close to the walls." He stops there. "Don't sleep near it. Don't put it near the fire you sleep by."

He leaves it at that, and his face says he's finished with it.

To Sefa, about the sum, he's quicker. He has clearly worked it out in his head more nights than one. "Three silver a day a man. The carter, five. Warden draws a gold." He takes the charcoal back from Bram and writes the figures down the margin of the claim sheet. "Twenty-one days. A hundred and twenty-six gold, near enough. That's the number." He doesn't argue about seventeen and sixteen. He puts the stone back on the sheet and leaves it where Sefa can take it when she means to.

Bram lifts the case down off the shelf. He sets it on top of his pack under the flap and lashes it across with his own rope, keeping the rope clear of the sealed cord. He tests it with a shrug, and the box sits. "Your claim goes with us. Hope the next knock brings your wages." He steps out into the light. Osric watches the box go through the door as if it were a tooth coming out.

Pell is already outside. The sun is well up over the eastern lip of the cut and the western hills are hard and clear. There's time enough for half a day of road if nobody dawdles. He walks toward the head of the track, where the yard runs along the edge of the lower cut and he can see down the hill. There's nothing on the track. Their own three sets of prints come up it, and the crowd's prints go down it. Nothing has come since.

The ground under him has been walked on for a hundred years. Ten feet short of the track, it cracks.

He hears it before he feels it, a dry punky sound like a rotten plank. Then the chalk crust he's standing on folds inward. Below it there's old timber and nothing under the timber, and Pell goes through.

It's eight feet of falling, and then water. It's black and cold enough to knock the breath out of him. He hits something hard on the way down: a shoulder, a hip, the edge of a ledge. It bruises and jars him but breaks nothing. A rain of chalk, rotten beam-ends and loose stone comes down after him. One of the stones is a squared block as big as a cask. It drops past his shoulder and lands on his left leg below the knee, under the water, and pins it to the floor.

When the splashing stops, Pell is standing, or half-standing, in water up to his chest. His leg is held fast under the stone. The cold is the deep-ground kind that goes into the bones quickly. A ragged hole of daylight hangs eight feet above him, with dust still sifting through it into the water. By that light he can see he's in a cut chamber, an old working with its walls squared by hand. Here and there in the wet stone a faint crust catches the light, pinkish white, like frost on a cellar wall. The chamber runs back past where the light reaches. Somewhere in the dark water is trickling in. The air smells of stone and wet. Under that there's something faintly sweet.

Up in the yard, Bram is twenty feet off when the ground folds, with the case on his back. He turns in time to see Pell's head and shoulders vanish, and he hears the splash come up out of the hole. Inside the house, Sefa hears the crack and the rumble of loose stone. She hears Osric's chair go over behind her.

The warden is in the doorway before she is. He stops there with one hand on the frame and looks at the hole in his yard. All the colour has gone out of his face.

"That's the old low cut," he says, to nobody. "That runs under there."

Down in the hole the water settles around Pell's chest, still and very cold.

“Pell! Can you hear me?” I call. “Sefa, mind the edge—the ground may still go!”

I crouch where I am and set my pack down carefully, freeing the rope from the case and leaving both well back from the collapse.

“Osric, is there a sound way into that cut?”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa steps out beside Osric, close but not crowding him, and keeps her voice steady so it doesn't carry far across the yard.

"Easy, Osric. Breathe." She peers toward the collapse, body angled against the dust still rolling out of the old cut, one hand half-raised to keep the others from wandering closer. "Was anyone still working down there yesterday when the bell went? Any of the lads, the carter, anybody at all? And that old low cut—does it run under the yard we're standing on, or only under the quarry face?"

messages.text:
The first thing I do is not shout. Shouting means breathing, and the air down here is sweet, and Osric just told us what sweet means. I pull the wet collar of my shirt up over my nose and mouth and breathe through it, shallow, and I keep my head as high above the water as I can get it.

Then I shout — once, short, up at the hole: "Bram! Sefa! Hole in the yard, ten feet short of the track — I'm in water, leg's pinned. Don't come to the edge, the crust's rotten. Rope — mine's in my pack, fifty feet of silk. And Sefa, don't breathe deep down here. The salts are on the walls."

While they sort themselves out I get to work on the leg. I feel down through the water with both hands to find the shape of the block — which edge is on me, whether it's resting on a ledge or flat on the floor, if there's any rock of my own I can get under it as a lever. I'm not trying to lift twenty stone of chalk with my back. I'm looking for whether I can twist the leg out from under it sideways, boot and all, or whether the boot comes off and the leg follows.

If the block won't shift and the leg won't slide, I brace my free foot against the wall, get both hands on the top edge, and try to rock it off my shin rather than lift it — a block that dropped is a block that can roll.

And I keep one ear on the dark end of the chamber, where the water's trickling in, because I didn't like the word "flooded" and I like it less with my leg under a rock.

You pull the wet collar of your shirt up over your nose and mouth and breathe through the cloth, short and shallow. Wet linen and cold stone, and under them the sweetness, faint and stale like a cellar where something once was stored. You tip your head back as far as your neck will go and shout once.

The chamber throws your voice back at you off the squared walls. Above, chalk dust drifts through the light. A moment later a loop of hemp rope slaps the water a foot from your shoulder and floats there, with the rest of it running up taut over the broken lip. Somebody up there is holding it.

Then you feel for the leg.

The water is black past your ribs, but your hands find the block. It's squared work, smooth on top, about the size of a cask. It hasn't settled flat on the floor. One corner is propped on something under the silt, so it sits tilted, with its lower edge across your shin below the knee. That edge isn't dressed like the rest. It's rough and jagged where it broke off, and when your fingers follow it down to your leg they come away sliding over cloth that's torn, and over what's under the cloth. It doesn't hurt yet, because the cold is taking care of that, but you know how a wound feels. The edge has gone into your calf, and the block's weight is what's holding it shut. Once that stone comes off, the leg will bleed hard, straight away and into cold water. You'll need a healing ready the moment it moves, a potion down your throat or a hand of light on you, or the bleeding will take you under.

Your hands find something else on the way across the top of the block. The face toward you isn't plain. There are cut lines in it, deep and regular, running out from a round boss in the middle like spokes. All around them, in a ring, are rows of small hard-cut marks, short strokes and notches, set close together like a tally.

You feel along the leg for a way to twist it out sideways. The block has it trapped at the shin and there's no slack, boot or no boot. So you do what you said you'd do. You plant your free foot against the wall behind you, get both hands over the top edge, and throw your weight into rocking it, trying to roll it off the corner it's propped on.

Wet linen and cold stone, and under them the sweetness, faint and stale like a cellar where something once was stored. He tips his head back as far as his neck will go and shouts once.

The chamber throws his voice back at him off the squared walls. Above, chalk dust drifts through the light. A moment later a loop of hemp rope slaps the water a foot from his shoulder and floats there, with the rest of it running up taut over the broken lip. Somebody up there is holding it.

Then he feels for the leg.

The water is black past his ribs, but his hands find the block. It's squared work, smooth on top, about the size of a cask. It hasn't settled flat on the floor. One corner is propped on something under the silt, so it sits tilted, with its lower edge across his shin below the knee. That edge isn't dressed like the rest. It's rough and jagged where it broke off, and when his fingers follow it down to his leg they come away sliding over cloth that's torn, and over what's under the cloth. It doesn't hurt yet, because the cold is taking care of that, but he knows how a wound feels. The edge has gone into his calf, and the block's weight is what's holding it shut. **Once that stone comes off, the leg will bleed hard, straight away and into cold water. He'll need a healing ready the moment it moves, a potion down his throat or a hand of light on him, or the bleeding will take him under.**

His hands find something else on the way across the top of the block. The face toward him isn't plain. There are cut lines in it, deep and regular, running out from a round boss in the middle like spokes. All around them, in a ring, are rows of small hard-cut marks, short strokes and notches, set close together like a tally.

He feels along the leg for a way to twist it out sideways. The block has it trapped at the shin and there's no slack, boot or no boot. So he does what he said he'd do. He plants his free foot against the wall behind him, gets both hands over the top edge, and throws his weight into rocking it, trying to roll it off the corner it's propped on.

opening.narration:
The cart track bends one last time, and Whitestone opens up before you: a white wound in the hillside, terraces of chalky stone glaring in the late-morning sun, dust drifting across a yard of spoil heaps and sheds. Pell Dunmore, Bram Halloway and Sefa Marrin have covered half a day of road since before dawn, and somewhere behind them, half a day back, Maela Thorn's shop waits for a sealed case that must reach it before sunset.

But the quarry does not sound like a quarry. No ring of picks, no shouting from the faces, no creak from the lifting frame. Hammers and wedges lie scattered near the lower cut as if their owners simply set them down and walked away. A stone cart stands half-loaded, its traces empty, no mule in sight. Only the chimney of the low slate-roofed house shows life — a thin grey thread of smoke.

In the doorway of that house stands a heavy-set man in a dust-whitened leather apron, a ring of keys at his belt. He has already seen you. He does not wave and he does not come forward; he just stands there, arms folded, waiting to see what you do next.

screens.text:
The session begins.

The cart track bends one last time, and Whitestone opens up before you: a white wound in the hillside, terraces of chalky stone glaring in the late-morning sun, dust drifting across a yard of spoil heaps and sheds. You, Pell Dunmore and Sefa Marrin have covered half a day of road since before dawn, and half a day back, Maela Thorn's shop waits for a sealed case that must reach it before sunset.

But the quarry does not sound like a quarry. No ring of picks, no shouting from the faces, no creak from the lifting frame. Hammers and wedges lie scattered near the lower cut as if their owners simply set them down and walked away. A stone cart stands half-loaded, its traces empty, no mule in sight. Only the chimney of the low slate-roofed house shows life, a thin grey thread of smoke.

In the doorway of that house stands a heavy-set man in a dust-whitened leather apron, a ring of keys at his belt. He has already seen you. He does not wave and he does not come forward; he just stands there, arms folded, waiting to see what you do next.

Your records:
Bram Halloway — Human, fighter 5 (Champion; Protection fighting style), former caravan guard of the Trade Way, level 5
HP 44/44 · AC 18 · Speed 30 feet
STR 17 · DEX 12 · CON 15 · INT 10 · WIS 13 · CHA 10
Skills: Athletics +6; Perception +4; Survival +4; Intimidation +3; Tools: land vehicles +3
Saves: Strength saving throw +6 (proficient); Constitution saving throw +5 (proficient); Dexterity saving throw +1; Intelligence saving throw +0; Wisdom saving throw +1; Charisma saving throw +0
Attacks: Longsword +6 to hit, 1d8+3 slashing (1d10+3 two-handed); Javelin +6 to hit, 1d6+3 piercing, range 30/120; Extra Attack: two attacks with the Attack action
Abilities: Proficiency bonus +3; Extra Attack: attacks twice when taking the Attack action; Fighting style, Protection: with a shield, a reaction imposes disadvantage on an attack against a creature within 5 feet of him; Second Wind: a bonus action, regains 1d10+5 hit points; once per short rest; Action Surge: one additional action on his turn; once per short rest; Improved Critical (Champion): a weapon attack crits on 19 or 20; Healer's kit: stabilises a dying creature without a check (ten uses)
Limits: No magic at all; Heavy armour: disadvantage on Stealth; Second Wind and Action Surge return only after a short rest
Counters: Hit dice 5/5; Second wind 1/1; Action surge 1/1; Heroic inspiration 0/1
Money: 23 gp; 14 sp; 30 cp
Worn: Armor / clothing: Chain Mail; Main hand: Longsword; Off hand: Shield
Pack: Bedroll and Hardtack; Healer's Kit; Hempen Rope (50 feet); Javelin ×4; Tinderbox; Torch ×3

Where you are: at the edge of Whitestone quarry yard, facing the slate-roofed house · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 1 — what does Bram Halloway do?

You remark quietly to Pell and Sefa that the quarry is unnaturally still for a working day. Pell, a half-step behind you now, keeps his thumbs hooked in his belt and murmurs to you both that nobody has run for the road and the tools were dropped, not packed, and that he wants to see whether the man says the word "case" before you do. Sefa, keeping her hands open and clear of her dagger, says low that hammers don't get left like that unless their owners fled or were taken.

You walk toward the house, shield low, sword sheathed, watching the sheds and the lower cut. Nothing lurks behind the spoil heaps, and nothing moves on the lifting frame except a loose rope end turning in the breeze. Every shed door is shut but one: a low lean-to at the lip of the lower cut, its plank door standing a hand's width open.

The man in the doorway has no blade. A mason's mallet hangs from a peg inside the doorframe, within easy reach if he wanted it.

You stop a few paces short and leave his doorway clear. The man notices that. You give your name, say Maela Thorn sent you for a sealed case of dye-salts, and ask if he's the warden. You glance at the abandoned cart and ask whether work has stopped for the day or something is wrong. Behind you, Pell stops twenty feet off and gives the man an easy nod, saying Thorn's shop in Beregost sent you and it's a quiet day. Sefa steps forward beside you and warmly says you come from Maela Thorn's shop on the Trade Way, that she expects a sealed case from the Whitestone warden by sunset, and asks if that's him.

"Osric Hale. Warden." His voice is low and flat, and he doesn't add to it. He looks past you at the cart with its empty traces. "Stopped yesterday. Noon bell. They walked." A pause. "Three weeks and not a copper from the Gate. I'd have gone with them, if it were mine to walk off."

He tips his chin at the hammers scattered by the lower cut. "Those are the house's tools. They left them where the house can find them. Carter took the mule. He was owed most."

"Case is inside," Osric says. "Sealed, the way she wanted it." He doesn't step aside. He rubs a thumb across the dust on his fingers, slowly. "Before it goes anywhere, I want to know something. Your Thorn. Has she paid for it already? And who did she pay?" His jaw works once. "Because it wasn't me. And it wasn't my lads."

Behind him the room is dim. There's a table, a cold mug, a ledger lying open under a stone, and a fire burning low in the grate.

Your journal, new:
+ Goal: The Whitestone Case
+ Quest: The Whitestone Case
+ Thread: Osric's Unpaid Wages

Where you are: quarry yard, a few paces from the warden's doorway · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 2 — what does Bram Halloway do?

Sefa speaks after you, holding Osric's gaze. She says she doesn't know either, that Thorn pays only when the case is in her hands, and that she won't lie to get past him. She offers a witness: Osric can walk with you all to Beregost and ask Thorn himself before the buyer's coach leaves, or, if the quarry can't spare him, she will carry his question to Thorn in his name and bring back the answer. She asks who should have paid him, the quarry's owner or a factor in the Gate.

Pell speaks next. He points at the open ledger and gives his reading of the house in the Gate, Thorn's coin and the unpaid wages. He proposes that the case go to Beregost today, that Osric write down what he's owed on a sheet from the ledger, and that Pell put it in Thorn's hand himself. He says plainly that he isn't offering Osric your ninety, but that he'd put Osric's keeping the fire going and the door shut on the sheet too.

Osric hears all three of you out without moving. When you say you won't invent an answer, the warden's jaw loosens a little. When Sefa says the same in different words, he looks at her again, longer this time.

"Vandarren," Osric says, answering you. "House Vandarren. They own Whitestone on paper. Their factor in the Gate takes the sales, and the wages are supposed to come back down through him." He moves his head slightly toward the ledger. "Four letters I've sent him. Nothing came back. No coin, no reply." He looks at you. "Nothing's owing on the case from me. Salt's cut, sealed, ready. The price is the house's business, and I don't see it. I'm holding it because it's the only thing at Whitestone anyone wants. That's all."

He turns to Sefa. "Can't walk to Beregost with you. If I leave the gate the house says I abandoned the quarry, and then there's no wages for anybody, ever." He takes that in for a moment, then gives a short nod. "You put the question to her in my name, though. That I'll take."

When Pell talks of someone less polite coming for the case, Osric's mouth goes tight, but he doesn't argue. Then Pell mentions the sheet, and the warden takes his weight off the doorframe for the first time since you came up the track.

"Written down," he says. "Aye. A thing written down goes further than me shouting at a coach." He looks at Pell a moment. "Fifteen men and a carter. Twenty-one days. Plus what I'm owed, if you'll put it on." He doesn't say thank you.

Then he steps out of the door and leaves it open behind him.

He goes in to the table, lifts the stone off the open ledger, turns to the back, and draws a stub of charcoal from his apron. From the doorway the room is plainer now. There's a cot against the far wall with the blanket still folded square, and a shelf above the grate. On the shelf sits a squat box of dark wood about a foot and a half long, bound at the corners with iron, with three blobs of red wax pressed over the clasp and cord. Osric sits down heavily in front of the ledger. He doesn't write fast. His lips move with the names as he puts them down one under another, the charcoal scratching. Outside, the loose rope end on the lifting frame turns slowly in the wind, and a little chalk dust lifts off the yard and settles again.

Your journal, new:
+ Promise: Osric's Question and Claim

Where you are: Doorway of the warden's hut at Whitestone quarry, with Osric inside writing · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 3 — what does Bram Halloway do?

Sefa stops just inside the door, out of the wind, and asks Osric to name the Vandarren factor in the Gate. She says she wants to know whose name to watch when she studies Thorn's face. She adds that she will carry the sheet herself and put it directly into Thorn's hands. Pell keeps away from the table so as not to crowd the writing. He asks leave to look the case over without opening it, so he knows how the seals looked when he took it. While he handles it he asks whether the factor has a name and whether anyone else knows the case is on the shelf. Afterward he says the sun is already past the quarter and the road needs thinking about.

Osric's charcoal stops at Sefa's question.

"Pryce. Haddon Pryce." He says it like a man spitting grit. "Keeps a room off the Wide, over a chandler's. Takes the house's sales, sends the wages down. Supposed to." He writes it at the top of the sheet in square, careful letters and looks at Sefa once. "Watch her face, then. I'd like to know what it does."

You ask for the dates. Osric grunts and turns pages back through the ledger, past years of tallies: blocks cut, carts loaded, men's names with small marks beside them. He copies four dates under Pryce's name, one for each tenday, the last three days old. "Hears it," he repeats after you, flat. "Aye. That's what I'm buying."

When Pell asks about the case, Osric jerks his chin at the shelf. "Look. Keep it where I can see it."

Pell lifts it down slowly and holds it in the light from the door, and you lean in beside him. The box gives him nothing to worry about. The cord goes once around the body and once through the clasp, all one piece, with no cut or re-tied knot. Three seals in red wax sit flat and clean, and the edges have never been lifted. All three carry the same small mark: a mason's square over a W. Among the iron keys on the ring at Osric's belt hangs a stubby brass seal with the same square cut into its face. The iron corners have rust in their nail-heads and no fresh bright scratches. The hinges have never been pried. The box is heavier than it looks, maybe twenty-five pounds. When Pell tilts it, the weight inside slides a little with a dry, slow hiss like coarse salt in a sack. Nothing clinks.

You judge it against your pack. It's too long to go inside. Strapped on top under the flap and lashed at the cord, it will ride well enough, as long as nobody runs.

"Who knows it's here?" Osric repeats Pell's question back to himself. "My lads. The carter. Pryce, he wrote the order. Your Thorn." He thinks about it. "Nobody's come up the track but you three. I'd have seen."

You ask how to carry it, and the warden takes a moment over that one.

"Dry. Damp cakes it." The charcoal goes on scratching. "And keep it off a fire." He doesn't say why. He writes the last line, his own name under sixteen others, with *twenty-one days* beside it. Then he looks at your offer of a receipt as if it were a strange tool he's deciding whether to trust.

"Receipt." He tears the sheet out along the stitching, carefully, and pushes the ledger an inch across the table toward the door, back pages open and blank. "Under the names, then. In the house's book. So it's on record who took it."

He lays the torn claim sheet where the case sat, puts the stone on it to keep the draught from lifting it, and rests his flat, dusty hand beside it. Pell sets the box back on the shelf exactly where it was. In the grate a log settles and gives off a little smoke, and outside the sun has climbed clear of the eastern lip of the cut.

Where you are: inside Osric's hut, near the door · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 4 — what does Bram Halloway do?

You take the charcoal and write the receipt slowly. Osric leans across unasked and puts the date above it in his square hand. You write that you collected from Osric Hale, for delivery to Maela Thorn of Beregost, one closed wooden case with the cord uncut and three Whitestone wax seals intact, contents not inspected, and you sign it. Pell bends over the book after you and writes his name below, plain, with no flourish. Osric reads both lines, reads the last one twice, and nods once.

Pell's question about the salts and Sefa's about the same thing get a single answer. Osric looks at the box rather than at either of them. It isn't a carter's rule, he says. Burn a crumb and the smoke is sweet and heavy, and it sits in your head like a long day. The low-cut lads used to come up yawning when the lamps hung close to the walls. Don't sleep near it, and don't put it near the fire you sleep by. His face says he's finished.

To Sefa he is quicker about the sum. He takes the charcoal back from you and writes figures down the margin of the claim sheet: three silver a day a man, five for the carter, a gold for the warden. Over twenty-one days it comes to a hundred and twenty-six gold, near enough. He doesn't argue about seventeen names and sixteen. He sets the stone back on the sheet where Sefa can take it.

You lift the case down, set it on top of your pack under the flap and lash it across with your own rope, clear of the sealed cord. You test it with a shrug and the box sits. You tell Osric the claim goes with you and hope the next knock brings his wages, then step out into the light. Osric watches the box go through the door as if it were a tooth coming out.

Pell is already outside, walking toward the head of the track where the yard runs along the edge of the lower cut. The sun is well up over the eastern lip and there is time enough for half a day of road. Nothing is on the track but your own prints going up and the crowd's going down.

You are twenty feet off, the case on your back, when the ground folds. You turn in time to see Pell's head and shoulders vanish, and you hear the splash come up out of the hole.

Sefa and Osric come to the doorway behind you. Osric stops there with one hand on the frame, looks at the hole in his yard, and the colour goes out of his face. "That's the old low cut," he says, to nobody. "That runs under there."

Your records, changed:
Carried: + Sealed Case of Dye-Salts

Where you are: in the yard, near the hole · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 5 — what does Bram Halloway do?

Sefa moved up beside Osric and spoke to him quietly, telling him to breathe. She asked whether anyone had still been working down there the day before, and whether the old low cut ran under the yard or only under the quarry face.

You drop to a crouch where you stand. You unlash your rope from the box without touching the sealed cord, and set the pack and the case down a good fifteen feet back on hard ground. Then you call Pell's name down the hole.

The answer that comes back up is the hollow slap of water against stone, carried and doubled by the chamber.

Osric draws a breath as if he'd forgotten how, his eyes on the hole. Nobody has worked the low cut in three years, he says, too fast, and then he hears it and stops. When he goes on he's flat again. It runs under the yard, under the lean-to, and out to the old face below. He jerks his chin toward the low shed at the lip of the lower cut, its door a hand's width open. There's a boarded adit behind it, and he has the key.

You go forward on your knees, keeping your weight low. Osric's voice comes sharp from the doorway. "Left. Keep left of it. That's rock under. Right side's fill." He doesn't come out of the door to show you.

The session begins.

The cart track bends one last time, and Whitestone opens up before you: a white wound in the hillside, terraces of chalky stone glaring in the late-morning sun, dust drifting across a yard of spoil heaps and sheds. You, Pell Dunmore and Bram Halloway have covered half a day of road since before dawn, and half a day back, Maela Thorn's shop waits for a sealed case that must reach it before sunset.

But the quarry does not sound like a quarry. No ring of picks, no shouting from the faces, no creak from the lifting frame. Hammers and wedges lie scattered near the lower cut as if their owners simply set them down and walked away. A stone cart stands half-loaded, its traces empty, no mule in sight. Only the chimney of the low slate-roofed house shows life, a thin grey thread of smoke.

In the doorway of that house stands a heavy-set man in a dust-whitened leather apron, a ring of keys at his belt. He has already seen you. He does not wave and he does not come forward; he just stands there, arms folded, waiting to see what you do next.

Your records:
Sefa Marrin — Human, warlock 5 (The Celestial — the Lantern; Pact of the Tome), former hospice novice, level 5
HP 38/38 · AC 14 · Speed 30 feet
STR 8 · DEX 14 · CON 14 · INT 12 · WIS 10 · CHA 18
Skills: Persuasion +7; Arcana +4; Religion +4; Insight +3
Saves: Wisdom saving throw +3 (proficient); Charisma saving throw +7 (proficient); Strength saving throw −1; Dexterity saving throw +2; Constitution saving throw +2; Intelligence saving throw +1
Attacks: Eldritch Blast +7 to hit, two beams, 1d10+4 force each, range 120 feet; Dagger +5 to hit, 1d4+2 piercing, thrown 20/60
Abilities: Proficiency bonus +3; Spell attack +7; spell save DC 15; Pact Magic: two 3rd-level pact slots, recovered only on a short or long rest; Healing Light: a pool of six d6 per long rest; a bonus action spends up to four dice to heal a creature within 60 feet; Pact of the Tome: the Book of Shadows holds three extra cantrips (Guidance, Spare the Dying, Thaumaturgy); Agonizing Blast: +4 to each Eldritch Blast beam's damage; Repelling Blast: a beam that hits pushes the target up to 10 feet away; Eyes of the Rune Keeper: reads all writing
Spells: Eldritch Blast (cantrip); Light (cantrip); Sacred Flame (cantrip); Mage Hand (cantrip); Minor Illusion (cantrip); Guidance (cantrip); Spare the Dying (cantrip); Thaumaturgy (cantrip); Cure Wounds (1); Guiding Bolt (1); Misty Step (2); Lesser Restoration (2); Hold Person (2); Daylight (3)
Limits: Two pact slots only, back only after a rest; Light armour; Strength 8 — weak up close; One concentration spell at a time
Counters: Hit dice 5/5; Pact slots 2/2; Healing light 6/6; Heroic inspiration 0/1
Money: 1 pp; 8 gp; 41 sp; 12 cp
Worn: Amulet: Prayer Beads; Armor / clothing: Studded Leather Armour; Belt: Book of Shadows; Main hand: Dagger
Pack: Bedroll and Rations; Candle ×2; Tinderbox

Where you are: at the edge of Whitestone quarry yard, facing the slate-roofed house · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 1 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

Quietly, you tell Pell and Bram that the quiet is wrong, that no one leaves hammers like that unless they left fast or were taken. Pell, who has dropped half a step back so Bram's shield leads, keeps his thumbs hooked in his belt and murmurs that nobody has run for the road, and that he wants to see whether the man says the word "case" before you do. Bram murmurs that it's quiet for a working quarry.

You keep your hands open and away from your dagger and step forward toward the house, calling out warmly that you come from Maela Thorn's shop on the Trade Way, that she expects a sealed case from the warden of Whitestone by sunset, and asking if that's him. Bram stops a few paces short of the doorway, leaving it clear, and gives his name; he says Maela Thorn sent you for a sealed case of dye-salts, asks if the man is the warden, and asks whether work has stopped for the day or something is wrong. Pell stops twenty feet off and gives the man an easy nod, saying Thorn's shop in Beregost sent you and it's a quiet day. The man nods back once and says nothing.

You watch him the whole time he talks. He has no blade, though a mason's mallet hangs from a peg inside the doorframe within easy reach. He isn't relaxed, and he isn't afraid either. He stands square in the door like a man who has decided what he's guarding and how far he'll move for it, which isn't far. His eyes are red-rimmed, like someone who sat up late with a lamp and a grievance. Your warmth doesn't soften him. It makes him look at you a moment longer than at the other two, as if he's weighing whether it's real.

"Osric Hale. Warden." His voice is low and flat, and he doesn't add to it. He looks past Bram at the cart with its empty traces. "Stopped yesterday. Noon bell. They walked." A pause. "Three weeks and not a copper from the Gate. I'd have gone with them, if it were mine to walk off."

He tips his chin at the hammers scattered by the lower cut. "Those are the house's tools. They left them where the house can find them. Carter took the mule. He was owed most."

"Case is inside," Osric says. "Sealed, the way she wanted it." He doesn't step aside. He rubs a thumb across the dust on his fingers, slowly. "Before it goes anywhere, I want to know something. Your Thorn. Has she paid for it already? And who did she pay?" His jaw works once. "Because it wasn't me. And it wasn't my lads."

Behind him the room is dim. There's a table, a cold mug, a ledger lying open under a stone, and a fire burning low in the grate.

Your journal, new:
+ Goal: The Whitestone Case
+ Quest: The Whitestone Case
+ Thread: Osric's Unpaid Wages

Where you are: quarry yard, a few paces from the warden's doorway · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 2 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

Bram answers first, plainly: he doesn't know. The woman who hired you wants the case collected, ninety gold between you on delivery before sunset, and she said nothing about who was paid for the salts. He says he won't make up an answer to get through the door, and that he has waited on wages himself. He nods at the ledger and asks Osric who owes his men, the quarry owners or Thorn, and whether anything is owing on this case or whether Osric is holding it against the missing wages.

You speak next, as you meant to.

Then Pell speaks. He says he doesn't know, points at the open ledger, and lays out his reading of the house in the Gate, Thorn's coin and the unpaid wages. He proposes that the case go to Beregost today, that Osric write down what he's owed on a sheet from the ledger, and that he put it in Thorn's hand himself. He says plainly that he isn't offering Osric your ninety, but that he'd put Osric's keeping the fire going and the door shut on the sheet too. While he talks he watches Osric.

Osric hears all three of you out without moving. When Bram says he won't invent an answer, the warden's jaw loosens a little. When you say the same in different words, he looks at you again, longer this time. His hands stay folded, and the right one never goes near the mallet on its peg.

"Vandarren," Osric says, answering Bram. "House Vandarren. They own Whitestone on paper. Their factor in the Gate takes the sales, and the wages are supposed to come back down through him." He moves his head slightly toward the ledger. "Four letters I've sent him. Nothing came back. No coin, no reply." He looks at Bram. "Nothing's owing on the case from me. Salt's cut, sealed, ready. The price is the house's business, and I don't see it. I'm holding it because it's the only thing at Whitestone anyone wants. That's all."

He turns to you. "Can't walk to Beregost with you. If I leave the gate the house says I abandoned the quarry, and then there's no wages for anybody, ever." He takes that in for a moment, then gives a short nod. "You put the question to her in my name, though. That I'll take."

When Pell talks of someone less polite coming for the case, Osric's mouth goes tight, but he doesn't argue. Then Pell mentions the sheet, and the warden takes his weight off the doorframe for the first time since you came up the track.

"Written down," he says. "Aye. A thing written down goes further than me shouting at a coach." He looks at Pell a moment. "Fifteen men and a carter. Twenty-one days. Plus what I'm owed, if you'll put it on." He doesn't say thank you.

Then he steps out of the door and leaves it open behind him.

He goes in to the table, lifts the stone off the open ledger, turns to the back, and draws a stub of charcoal from his apron. From the doorway the room is plainer now. There's a cot against the far wall with the blanket still folded square, and a shelf above the grate. On the shelf sits a squat box of dark wood about a foot and a half long, bound at the corners with iron, with three blobs of red wax pressed over the clasp and cord. Osric sits down heavily in front of the ledger. He doesn't write fast. His lips move with the names as he puts them down one under another, the charcoal scratching. Outside, the loose rope end on the lifting frame turns slowly in the wind, and a little chalk dust lifts off the yard and settles again.

Your journal, new:
+ Promise: Osric's Question and Claim

Where you are: Doorway of the warden's hut at Whitestone quarry, with Osric inside writing · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 3 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

Pell steps in after you and stays out of Osric's light. He asks to look at the case without opening it, saying he wants to know how the seals sat when he took it. While he handles it he asks Osric whether the factor has a name, and whether anyone else knows the case is on the shelf. Bram stays by the door. He asks Osric to put the dates of the letters under the factor's name, and says you can promise only that the claim will be heard, not that it will be paid. He also asks how the salts should be carried and offers a receipt saying who collected the case and that the seals were intact.

When you ask for the factor's name, Osric's charcoal stops.

"Pryce. Haddon Pryce." He says it like a man spitting grit. "Keeps a room off the Wide, over a chandler's. Takes the house's sales, sends the wages down. Supposed to." He writes it at the top of the sheet in square, careful letters and looks at you once. "Watch her face, then. I'd like to know what it does."

He turns back through the ledger, past years of tallies: blocks cut, carts loaded, men's names with small marks beside them. He copies four dates under Pryce's name, one for each tenday, the last three days old. "Hears it," he says flatly, repeating Bram. "Aye. That's what I'm buying."

He jerks his chin at the shelf when Pell asks about the case. "Look. Keep it where I can see it." Pell lifts it down and turns it in the light from the door, and Bram leans in beside him. Pell seems to find nothing wrong with it. The box is heavy, and the contents slide with a dry hiss like coarse salt. Bram judges it too long for his pack but says it could ride strapped on top.

"Who knows it's here?" Osric says. "My lads. The carter. Pryce, he wrote the order. Your Thorn." He thinks. "Nobody's come up the track but you three. I'd have seen."

On carrying it he says, "Dry. Damp cakes it," and, as the charcoal keeps scratching, "And keep it off a fire." He gives no reason. He writes his own name last under sixteen others, with *twenty-one days* beside it. He eyes the offer of a receipt as if it were a strange tool, then tears the sheet out along the stitching and pushes the ledger an inch toward the door, back pages open and blank. "Under the names, then. In the house's book. So it's on record who took it."

He lays the claim sheet where the case sat, weights it with a stone, and rests his flat, dusty hand beside it. Pell sets the box back exactly where it was. A log settles in the grate and gives off a little smoke. Outside, the sun has climbed clear of the eastern lip of the cut.

Where you are: inside the doorway of Osric's hut at the quarry · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 4 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

You step up to the table and read the claim sheet openly, running your eyes from the sixteen names down to Osric's own, with the four dates under Haddon Pryce. You ask for the sum to set beside it: what the wages should have come to, how much a day, in what coin. You also ask whether the warning about fire is a carter's rule for any dye or whether something in the box would settle badly with a flame. You say the claim goes into your own hand and then Maela Thorn's, and that you won't promise Osric coin, only that it won't be forgotten in a pocket.

Bram takes the charcoal and writes the receipt slowly. Osric leans across unasked and puts the date above it in his square hand. The receipt records that Bram took from Osric Hale, to be delivered to Maela Thorn of Beregost, a single closed wooden case, its cord uncut, with three Whitestone wax seals unbroken and the contents not inspected. He signs it Bram Halloway. Pell bends over the book after him and writes his own name below, plain, with no flourish. Osric reads both lines, reads the last one twice, and nods once.

He takes Pell's question and yours together, because they're the same question. It isn't a carter's rule, he says, looking at the box rather than at either of you. Burn a crumb and the smoke is sweet and heavy, and it sits in your head like a long day. The low-cut lads used to come up yawning when the lamps hung close to the walls. Don't sleep near it, and don't put it near the fire you sleep by. His face says he's finished with it.

To you he is quicker about the sum, as if he has worked it out more nights than one. He takes the charcoal back from Bram and writes figures down the margin of the claim sheet: three silver a day a man, five for the carter, a gold for the warden. Over twenty-one days it comes to a hundred and twenty-six gold, near enough. He doesn't argue about seventeen names and sixteen. He puts the stone back on the sheet and leaves it where you can take it when you mean to.

Bram lifts the case down, sets it on his pack and lashes it across with his own rope, clear of the sealed cord. He tells Osric the claim goes with you and hopes the next knock brings his wages, then steps out. Osric watches the box go through the door as if it were a tooth coming out. Pell is already outside.

Then you hear a crack and the rumble of loose stone. Osric's chair goes over behind you. The warden is in the doorway before you are. He stops there with one hand on the frame and looks at the hole in his yard, and all the colour goes out of his face.

"That's the old low cut," he says, to nobody. "That runs under there."

Where you are: in the doorway of the warden's house, with Osric · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 5 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

Bram called Pell's name, warned you to mind the edge, and crouched to set his pack and case down well back on hard ground. He freed his rope from the case and asked Osric whether there was a sound way into the cut. Then he began working toward the hole, low, meaning to look for Pell without putting weight on the lip.

Bram unlashes his rope from the box without touching the sealed cord, and sets the pack and the case down a good fifteen feet back on hard ground. Then he calls Pell's name down the hole.

The answer that comes back up is the hollow slap of water against stone, carried and doubled by the chamber.

You stand at Osric's shoulder with one hand half raised, and the warden draws a breath as if he'd forgotten how. His eyes don't leave the hole.

"Nobody," he says. "Nobody's worked the low cut. Not three years." The words come out too fast for him, and he hears it and stops. When he goes on he's flat again. "Runs under the yard. Under the lean-to. Out to the old face below." His chin jerks toward the low shed at the lip of the lower cut, its door a hand's width open. "There's an adit behind it. Boarded. I've the key."

You listen past him. The dust is still settling, and the rope-end on the lifting frame turns in the wind. From under the ground you can hear water running somewhere in the dark, the steady trickle Pell landed beside. No boot moves anywhere in the yard and no voice comes from the sheds. The only people at Whitestone are the ones you can see.

Bram goes forward on his knees and keeps his weight low. Osric's voice comes sharp from the doorway. "Left. Keep left of it. That's rock under. Right side's fill." He doesn't come out of the door to show him.

Bram keeps left, and stops a forearm's length back from the broken lip. He looks down, braces a knee against firm rock, ties a loop, and pays it down hand over hand, keeping the rest of the coil wrapped round his forearm and his weight set back on solid ground.

Behind you, Osric has come off his doorframe at last. He walks stiffly toward the lean-to, the keys at his belt clinking, and doesn't look at the hole as he passes it.

Where you are: in the yard near the collapse, where Osric stood · Time: Day 1 · morning

The session is over.

after.question: Was there something you wanted to do and didn't?
after.text:
Honestly, yes — three small things, mostly because the scene kept me in a careful, listening register:

1. **I wanted to step into the hut before the collapse and take a real look around.** Not to pry, but to see what a man guarding the only thing of value keeps within reach: the cold mug, the blanket folded square, whether there were fresh rations or empty ones, whether the fire had been tended or just left. Sefa spent years reading sickrooms by lamplight — she'd notice whether Osric has been sleeping or sitting up with his back to the wall.

2. **I wanted to ask Osric about the men themselves, not just the wages.** How many of the fifteen had families down in Beregost, whether any of them stayed behind, whether the carter had kin or a reason to be owed the most. It would have cost nothing, and it might have changed how hard Sefa carries that claim sheet — wages are one thing, but seventeen men who walked off without their hammers is another.

3. **Most of all, I wanted to press him on the fire warning before the ground opened.** Not because I think Osric is lying — he isn't — but because "don't sleep near it" and "the smoke sits in your head" is exactly the sort of thing a hospice novice would know to take seriously. I had half a sentence for it and let it go because time mattered. Then Pell went missing, and the sentence died.

None of it was wasted. The scene worked because everybody held back a little. But Sefa left Whitestone — or rather, hasn't left it — with more questions than she's admitted out loud, and one of them is about that dark box riding on Bram's back.

For next session: if we get a moment before going down after Pell, I'd like Sefa to **cast Light** on something small and useful — a pebble, a coin, the rim of the hole — so the dark has a shape in it. She hasn't spent a single spell slot or even a cantrip yet, and standing over a collapsed floor with only daylight is exactly when the Lantern would want her to reach for light.

The session begins.

The cart track bends one last time, and Whitestone opens up before you: a white wound in the hillside, terraces of chalky stone glaring in the late-morning sun, dust drifting across a yard of spoil heaps and sheds. You, Bram Halloway and Sefa Marrin have covered half a day of road since before dawn, and half a day back, Maela Thorn's shop waits for a sealed case that must reach it before sunset.

But the quarry does not sound like a quarry. No ring of picks, no shouting from the faces, no creak from the lifting frame. Hammers and wedges lie scattered near the lower cut as if their owners simply set them down and walked away. A stone cart stands half-loaded, its traces empty, no mule in sight. Only the chimney of the low slate-roofed house shows life, a thin grey thread of smoke.

In the doorway of that house stands a heavy-set man in a dust-whitened leather apron, a ring of keys at his belt. He has already seen you. He does not wave and he does not come forward; he just stands there, arms folded, waiting to see what you do next.

HP 33/33 · AC 15 · Speed 30 feet
STR 10 · DEX 17 · CON 13 · INT 13 · WIS 12 · CHA 12
Skills: Stealth +9 (expertise); Sleight of Hand +6; Acrobatics +6; Perception +4; Investigation +4; Insight +4; Tools: thieves' tools +9 (expertise)

Where you are: at the edge of Whitestone quarry yard, facing the slate-roofed house · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 1 — what does Pell Dunmore do?

You drop half a step back so that Bram's shield leads, and cross the yard with your thumbs hooked in your belt, eyes off the man in the doorway and on everything else. Low, you tell the others that the quiet worries you, and that you want to see whether he says the word "case" before they do. Bram murmurs that it is quiet for a working quarry. Sefa adds, just as quietly, that men only leave their hammers lying like that if they fled in a hurry or were taken.

There's nothing hidden in the yard. Nobody is lying behind the spoil heaps, and nothing moves on the lifting frame except a loose rope end turning in the breeze. Every shed door is shut but one: a low lean-to at the lip of the lower cut, its plank door standing a hand's width open. The chalk dust has kept a day of footprints. Fifteen or twenty men walked across the yard from the faces and the sheds, all heading the same way, and joined the cart track west toward Beregost. They didn't run. The prints are even and close together, the way men walk in a crowd. A mule's hoofprints go with them. Nothing came back up the road except the three of you.

The man in the doorway wears no blade. A mason's mallet hangs from a peg inside the doorframe, within easy reach. His knuckles are thick and old-scarred, with white dust worked into the creases, but there are no fresh cuts or swelling.

Twenty feet off you stop, give him an easy nod, and say good morning, warden, that Thorn's shop in Beregost sent you, and that it's a quiet day. He nods back once and says nothing.

Bram stops a few paces short of him and leaves the doorway clear. He gives his name and says Maela Thorn sent you for a sealed case of dye-salts, asks if the man is the warden, and asks whether work has stopped for the day or something is wrong. Sefa steps forward too, hands open and away from her dagger, and warmly says you come from Maela Thorn's shop on the Trade Way, that she is expecting the warden of Whitestone to hand over a sealed case, wanted by sunset, and asks if that's him.

"Osric Hale. Warden." His voice is low and flat. He looks past Bram at the cart with its empty traces. "Stopped yesterday. Noon bell. They walked." A pause. "Three weeks and not a copper from the Gate. I'd have gone with them, if it were mine to walk off."

He tips his chin at the hammers scattered by the lower cut. "Those are the house's tools. They left them where the house can find them. Carter took the mule. He was owed most."

"Case is inside," Osric says. "Sealed, the way she wanted it." He doesn't step aside. He rubs a thumb across the dust on his fingers, slowly. "Before it goes anywhere, I want to know something. Your Thorn. Has she paid for it already? And who did she pay?" His jaw works once. "Because it wasn't me. And it wasn't my lads."

Behind him the room is dim. There's a table, a cold mug, a ledger lying open under a stone, and a fire burning low in the grate.

Your journal, new:
+ Goal: The Whitestone Case
+ Quest: The Whitestone Case
+ Thread: Osric's Unpaid Wages

Where you are: quarry yard, twenty feet from the warden's doorway · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 2 — what does Pell Dunmore do?

Bram answers first, plainly: he doesn't know. The woman who hired the three of you wants the case collected, ninety gold between you on delivery before sunset, and she said nothing about who was paid for the salts. He says he won't make up an answer just to get through the door, and that he has waited on wages himself. Then he nods at the ledger and asks Osric who owes his men, the quarry owners or Thorn, and whether anything is owing on this case or whether Osric is holding it against the missing wages.

Sefa follows, holding Osric's gaze. She says she doesn't know either, that Thorn pays only when the case is in her hands, and that she refuses to lie in order to get past him. She offers a witness: Osric can walk with you to Beregost and ask Thorn himself before the buyer's coach leaves, with all three of you there to say you saw him ask. If the quarry can't spare him, she will carry his question to Thorn in his name and bring back the answer, whatever it is. She adds that standing here till sunset gets none of you anything, and asks who should have paid him, the quarry's owner or a factor in the Gate.

Then you speak: you tell Osric you don't know, point out the open ledger, and lay out your reading of the Gate house, Thorn's coin and the unpaid wages. You propose that the case go to Beregost today, that he write down what he's owed on a sheet from the ledger, and that you put it in Thorn's hand yourself. You say plainly that you aren't offering him your ninety, but that you'd put his keeping the fire going and the door shut on the sheet too.

Osric hears all three of you out without moving. When Bram says he won't make up an answer, the warden's jaw loosens a little. When Sefa says the same in different words, he looks at her again, longer this time. While you talk, you watch his hands. They stay folded, and the right one never goes near the mallet on its peg.

You are also watching what's under the anger.
